text.en: The children in the picture are measuring a tree and a wall. What are they finding out: length, height, breadth, depth, weight or temperature? Length, height, breadth and depth all tell us a length. In this chapter you will measure using metre ropes and centimetre scales, estimate lengths, and find the perimeter of shapes.

Tall, short, long, wide, deep, high and broad are all words used in daily life for different lengths. Height, width, breadth and depth all measure length. We use different words in different situations, but they are all lengths. Weight and temperature are not lengths. They are measured with other tools. Measure the height of a student with a measuring tape or a metre rope. Other tools can also measure height, like a ruler or a scale. In Class 3 we learned that length is measured in metres. Most Class 4 children are more than one metre tall. The height of a door is more than a metre, but your arm is less than a metre.
We can make ropes of 1 metre, half a metre and a quarter of a metre. Two half-metre ropes make a one-metre rope, and four quarter-metre ropes make a one-metre rope. Written as numbers: 1 m = 1/2 m + 1/2 m, 1 m = 1/4 m + 1/4 m + 1/4 m + 1/4 m, and 1/2 m = 1/4 m + 1/4 m. Use the ropes to make lines of 1 m, 5 m and 10 m on the floor by placing the metre rope again and again. Walk, jump and crawl along them to get a feel for how big 5 m and 10 m are. Measure a long jump with the ropes, and find who jumped the longest and who jumped the shortest. First estimate, then measure and check how close you were. Estimate the length and breadth of your classroom, then measure it. Practise: 100 metres takes about as many footsteps as you count by walking along it.
A blue whale is about 30 metres long. A bus is about 10 metres long, and a cricket bat is about 1 metre. So we can compare animals using familiar things. Two blue whales are about 60 metres, which is as long as 6 buses. One whale is as long as 30 cricket bats. A crocodile is about 6 metres long, so 5 crocodiles are about as long as one blue whale. Two ostriches stand about as tall as a giraffe is. When we compare to known lengths, we can make a good guess about an unknown length.
A metre is too long to measure small things like an eraser or a grain of rice. We need a smaller unit called the centimetre, written cm. A metre scale is divided into 100 equal parts. The length of each part is one centimetre. Look at a measuring tape. The distance between two marks is 1 cm. The numbers show how many centimetres so far. The red bar of 1 cm repeated 10 times is 10 cm. 100 small bars of 1 cm make a metre. So 1 metre = 100 centimetres. Children often think the 100 on the tape is the number of marks, but it is the number of centimetre gaps. We start measuring from 0, not from the edge of the scale if the scale has a gap at the end. Chutki can measure her plant every week and note down how many centimetres it has grown.
Place the zero mark of the scale at one end of the object and read the number at the other end. That number is the length in cm. Estimate before measuring. A fingernail is less than 1 cm wide, an eraser is more than 1 cm, an ant is about 1 cm or less, a grain of wheat is less than 1 cm and a rajma seed is more than 1 cm. Roll three toy cars down a ramp and measure how far each goes in centimetres. The car which goes the farthest has rank 1. In the treasure hunt we walk only on the tiles and go around obstacles. We measure each route in centimetres, and the shortest route is the one with the smallest number of cm. Trace your hand and measure its length. Then use the hand as a unit to estimate other things like your textbook, a chair or a desk and check with the scale. If a scale is broken at the start, we can still measure by subtracting. If an object starts at the 3 cm mark and ends at the 9 cm mark, its length is 9 − 3 = 6 cm.
1 m = 100 cm, 2 m = 200 cm, 4 m = 400 cm, 6 m = 600 cm and 8 m = 800 cm. A length like 1 m 40 cm is 100 + 40 = 140 cm. A length 4 m 60 cm is 460 cm. 2 m 30 cm = 230 cm and 5 m 50 cm = 550 cm. We can match the wells that have the same depth this way. Make a height table of children in the class, in cm and in m. 150 cm is 1 m 50 cm. Find the tallest and the shortest child, and count how many are taller or shorter than 1 m.
The length of the boundary of a shape is called its perimeter. Bhola builds a boundary of bricks around his vegetable garden. The number of bricks along the boundary tells him how long the boundary is. On a dot grid with 1 cm dots, we can count the cm along the boundary. For a rectangle 6 cm long and 4 cm wide, the perimeter is 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 cm. Two shapes can look different but have the same perimeter. We find out by counting the length of the boundary of each. To estimate the perimeter of a desk, a blackboard or a classroom floor, measure each side with a scale and add all the sides. You can draw three different shapes each with a perimeter of 20 cm.

problem.en: An object starts at the 4 cm mark and ends at the 11 cm mark on a scale. What is its length?

text.en: The scale does not start from zero for this object.

why.en: So we cannot just read the last number.

text.en: Length = 11 − 4 = 7 cm.

why.en: Subtract the start from the end.

text.en: The object is 7 cm long.

prompt.en: Explain what a metre and a centimetre are, how many centimetres make a metre, and what perimeter means.

commonMisconceptions.en: The 100 on the tape is the number of marks

points.en: Height, width, breadth and depth are all lengths.
A centimetre is used to measure small things.
Perimeter is the length of the boundary of a shape.
Estimating first helps us check our measurements.
